At 3:17 in the morning, the vending machine began dispensing apologies.

Not snacks. Not coffee. Apologies.

The first one arrived in the metal tray with a hollow clatter, folded into a paper square no larger than a coin. Mara, the night receptionist, assumed someone had slipped it through the chute as a joke. She unfolded it beneath the blue-white lobby lights.

*I’m sorry I pretended not to see you waving from the train.*

No name. No date. Just the sentence, written in green ink.

The lobby belonged to a hotel people used mostly when they were between places: between flights, between marriages, between one version of themselves and another. Its carpets were patterned to conceal stains. Its clocks showed the time in cities nobody in the building had visited. Outside, rain glazed the airport road.

Mara looked at the vending machine.

“Very funny,” she said.

The machine hummed. A spiral turned. Another paper square dropped.

*I’m sorry I kept the blue cup after you left.*

Mara checked behind the machine, then opened its service panel with the key kept under the desk. Rows of chips, candy bars, and bottled water waited in perfect innocence. No hidden printer. No prankster crouched inside.

Another clatter.

*I’m sorry I made you feel difficult when you were only telling the truth.*

That one irritated her. It was too polished, too universal, the kind of sentence printed on greeting cards for people who wanted forgiveness without specificity.

She left it in the tray.

At 3:40, a guest came down from the seventh floor. He was an old man in hotel slippers and a wool coat buttoned over striped pajamas.

“Do you sell ginger ale?” he asked.

“Usually.”

He inserted two coins and pressed B6. The machine considered him. Instead of ginger ale, it released a folded square.

The old man opened it.

His face changed.

Not dramatically. There was no gasp, no stagger. Something simply went out of alignment, as if a picture frame had been nudged crooked.

“What does it say?” Mara asked.

He folded the note again.

“Nothing meant for you.”

He returned to the elevator without asking for his coins.

By four, the machine had gathered a congregation.

A flight attendant received: *I’m sorry I was relieved when the test was negative.*

A taxi driver received: *I’m sorry, Papa, that I learned your language too late.*

A woman with wet hair stood for ten minutes holding: *I’m sorry I let everyone call you strong so I wouldn’t have to help you.*

Nobody got what they paid for. Nobody complained.

Some read their notes aloud. Others swallowed them, metaphorically or nearly. One man tore his into confetti and then crawled beneath the snack machine to retrieve every piece.

“Is it always like this?” a boy asked Mara. He was perhaps nine years old, traveling with a mother asleep upright on the lobby sofa.

“No,” Mara said. “Usually it steals your money.”

The boy fed it a coin.

The machine dropped a note.

*I’m sorry I told you the moon was following our car. I didn’t know you would spend years waiting for something to stay.*

The boy frowned.

“I don’t get it.”

“Maybe it’s not for you.”

“Then who?”

Mara had no answer.

At 4:26, the vending machine’s glow flickered. The crowd had thinned. Guests returned to their rooms carrying words that had not existed an hour before but were somehow overdue.

Mara stood alone before the glass.

She had avoided buying anything. This, she told herself, was because she knew better. Machines were only machines, even when they developed a talent for emotional trespassing.

But she also knew exactly whose apology she wanted.

Her sister had been dead for eleven years. There had been an argument in a kitchen. A slammed door. A drive in bad weather. For years Mara had sorted the facts like evidence, arranging and rearranging them to see whether blame changed shape when viewed from another angle.

She inserted a coin.

Pressed A1.

The machine whirred.

A packet of salted peanuts fell into the tray.

Mara stared at it.

“No,” she said.

She inserted another coin. Pressed C4.

A chocolate bar.

Again. Water.

Again. Pretzels.

Soon she was laughing—not because it was funny, but because grief, when cornered, sometimes escaped wearing laughter’s coat.

“You gave everyone else one,” she told the machine.

Its fluorescent interior buzzed.

“I’ve been waiting.”

Nothing.

She struck the glass with the heel of her hand. Candy trembled on its hooks.

Then, from somewhere deep inside, came the faint mechanical sound of paper moving.

A square dropped into the tray.

Mara reached for it, then stopped. Her hand hovered.

She had imagined this moment so many times that every possible sentence seemed insufficient.

*I’m sorry I left.*

*I’m sorry we fought.*

*I’m sorry you had to live.*

She unfolded the note.

The handwriting was hers.

*I’m sorry I believed surviving meant I had to keep punishing you.*

For a long time, Mara stood without moving.

Dawn began quietly at the lobby windows, turning the rain from black to silver. Airport shuttles sighed at the curb. Elevators opened. Phones rang. The world resumed its ordinary appetite.

At six, the manager arrived and found the vending machine unplugged.

“Broken?” he asked.

Mara looked at the shelves inside: chips, candy, water, everything in its assigned place.

“No,” she said.

She slipped the note into her pocket.

“Just empty.”
